medium.conteudo_html:
I Spent Weeks Building AI Skills Inside a Chat Window.

Here’s What Nobody Tells You About It.

A real story about building six connected AI skills entirely through conversation — the mistakes that shaped them, the day it almost disappeared, and what actually happens when a team asks: can everyone use this?

There’s a particular kind of dread that comes with opening a real RFP for the first time. Not the summary slide someone made for the kickoff call. The actual document: four hundred pages, split across a main body and a “detailed requirements” appendix that contradicts the main body in three places you won’t find until it’s too late. Somewhere in there is an application inventory, a spreadsheet with names like “eSuite/TIPS/QDOD” and “Aligne Registration,” and no column that reliably tells you which of those four hundred systems a real customer would ever touch, and which ones just move data around in the dark.

Next to that sits the incident data. Not one file, several, from different systems that don’t agree on what a “ticket” even is. One export calls something a Bug. Another calls the same kind of thing an Incident. A third has no type field at all, just a description and a date.

Somebody has to turn all of that into a staffing number, a price, and a leadership deck, by Thursday.

I spent a stretch of my working life doing exactly that, not once but as a repeating pattern, pursuit after pursuit, and at some point I stopped doing it by hand and started building something to do it with me. Not a script. Not a model I trained. A set of AI skills, built entirely inside a chat window, in plain English, over the course of dozens of conversations. This is the story of building that thing, breaking it, watching it break in ways I didn’t expect, and, more than once, catching a mistake right before it would have shipped.

Where it actually started: one skill, and a keyword list that lied to me

The first thing I tried to build was the simplest-sounding piece: read an RFP, read an application list, and tell me which applications were customer-facing. I figured a keyword list would get most of the way there — anything with “portal,” “customer,” “CRM” in the name, flag it.

It didn’t work. Not a little bit off. Genuinely wrong, on nearly half the real rows I tested it against. A payment-processing backend with no login screen anywhere near it turned out to be squarely customer-facing, because it was the exact system charging real people’s credit cards in real time. A tool literally named “Customer Nomination Portal” turned out, once I actually read what it did, to be nothing a customer ever touched. The name lied. The keyword list, trusting the name, lied right along with it.

That was the first real lesson, and it shaped everything after it: never classify anything from a label alone. Read the actual content. If the content doesn’t tell you enough, go look it up. If you still can’t tell, ask a human rather than guess and hope. I wrote that rule into the skill’s own instructions, in plain language, the way you’d write a note to a new colleague on their first day. And because it was instructions rather than code, I could watch it work — or fail — in real time, in the same conversation, and just… fix it. Rewrite the paragraph. Try again.

Six skills need a conductor

One skill turned into two, then six: one to classify the applications, one to read incident tickets and figure out how much of that work needed frontline triage versus deep specialist attention, one to turn that into an actual staffing estimate, one to price the commercial structure around it, one to research the client’s business and technology posture, and one to assemble everything into a single, leadership-ready brief.

Six skills that each did one real thing well immediately created a new problem: something had to decide which one ran when, in what order, and what to do if a step revealed something the plan hadn’t anticipated. That became the seventh piece — an orchestrator — and it does five real jobs, none of which is the actual work itself:

It validates — reads every file that gets uploaded, all the way through, not just the filename or the first column, before deciding what kind of data it’s actually looking at.

It plans — states the whole sequence of steps up front, in plain language, and waits for an actual yes before doing anything.

It gates — runs one step, watches what comes out of it, and only then moves to the next. If a step’s own internal question needs answering, the orchestrator doesn’t answer it on the user’s behalf just because the plan was already approved.

It produces — makes sure every artifact each step is supposed to generate actually gets generated, rather than quietly skipping the parts nobody explicitly asked to see again.

And it learns — when a real correction comes in, it writes that correction permanently into the right skill’s own file, not just into the current conversation, so the next run doesn’t repeat the same mistake.

Here’s the detail that took me a while to really sit with, and it’s the most honest thing I can tell you about how this actually works under the hood: none of that coordination happens through code calling code. There’s no function signature, no schema, no return value passed between the orchestrator and the classifier and the pricing skill. What actually happens is that one skill’s instructions contain a sentence that says, in effect, “go read this other skill’s own file, and follow what it says.” The model reads that sentence, fresh, every single time, and does exactly that. That’s the entire mechanism. Instructions calling instructions, held together by a model’s ability to read and follow them correctly, over and over, under real pressure, with real data.

Once you see that clearly, you stop thinking of this as “software” in the traditional sense. It’s closer to a very well-organized set of standard operating procedures, handed to someone extremely capable, extremely fast, and, this part matters, not always right the first time.

The part that actually took the longest: teaching it to catch its own mistakes

Building six skills that each technically worked was the easy part, in hindsight. The real work came after: running the pipeline against real, messy, contradictory data and finding the places where “technically correct instructions” still produced a wrong answer.

Two moments stand out, because they taught the same lesson twice, in two different disguises.

The first: a file’s own resolver-team field showed nothing but generic integration-team names, nothing that looked remotely connected to the specific system I was trying to analyze. On the strength of that one field, the natural move was to conclude the file was irrelevant and set it aside. Instead, I made myself read the actual ticket descriptions inside it. Buried in the free text, the exact system I was looking for was named, not once but hundreds of times, in job names and error messages that never showed up in any structured column at all.

The second, a few steps later: a different file’s own “type” field read as one specific kind of record, entirely, nothing else. Trusting that field would have meant treating the whole file as the wrong kind of data and excluding it. Reading the actual titles instead, the overwhelming majority of them carried a real, verifiable ticket number belonging to the exact record type I actually needed. The field was describing something else, which tool had logged it, not what it actually was.

Same lesson, twice: a structured field tells you how something was labeled by whoever filled it in. It doesn’t tell you what the thing actually is. The only way to know that is to read it.

What made this feel less like “using a tool” and more like mentoring someone was what happened next. I didn’t just fix the immediate problem and move on. I wrote the pattern — not the specific client details, just the shape of the mistake — permanently into that skill’s own instructions, as a named, generalized lesson: check the filename, check every column, read real content, before you decide a file doesn’t matter. The next time this pipeline runs, on a completely different pursuit, it starts already knowing not to make that exact mistake. That’s not a metaphor. That’s a paragraph of English, sitting in a file, that gets read into context every time the skill triggers.

Getting smarter has a real cost, and nobody tells you that part upfront

Here’s where I want to be honest rather than triumphant, because the honest version is more useful.

The mechanism for “getting smarter over time” in a system like this is, almost entirely, writing more into the instructions. Every lesson learned becomes another paragraph, another reference file, another thing the model has to read the next time the skill triggers. That’s not free. Across the life of this project, the working conversation eventually grew large enough that it needed to be compacted, summarized and compressed, just to stay usable. The system’s entire memory of its own history, at a certain point, became too heavy to carry around in full.

That’s a genuine trade-off, not a bug. The same mechanism that makes the system more careful over time also makes every future conversation start a little heavier. Nobody selling you on “AI that learns from its mistakes” mentions that the learning itself has a storage cost, paid in the currency of context, but it does, and it’s worth knowing before you build something the same way.

There’s a second, separate kind of memory worth naming, because it’s a genuinely different mechanism and it’s easy to conflate the two. Alongside the skill files themselves, a lightweight memory of past conversations can persist across sessions: a running sense of who you are, what you’re working on, what you’ve already told the system, carried forward without you having to repeat it. That’s not the same thing as a lesson written permanently into a skill’s own instructions. One is “the system remembers this specific fact about this specific situation.” The other is “the system now permanently behaves differently for everyone, forever.” Getting those two confused is an easy, costly mistake: treating a passing conversational note as if it were a permanent, generalized fix, or the reverse.

The day it almost disappeared

Somewhere past the halfway point of building this, I asked for a full backup — a zipped archive of every skill file, just to have a copy saved somewhere outside the working environment. It felt like a small, slightly paranoid ask at the time.

A while later, in a completely different working session, I went looking for those same skills and found four out of fourteen. The other ten, including the orchestrator itself and two of the six pipeline skills, were simply gone. Not corrupted. Not moved. Gone, the way a folder is gone after a machine gets wiped and rebuilt from a clean image, which is more or less exactly what had happened underneath, invisibly, between one working session and the next.

The backup zip, asked for on a hunch weeks earlier, was the only surviving, verified-complete copy of that work. I didn’t just trust that it existed. I opened it, extracted every file, and read the actual content back out before restoring anything, because “the zip file is the right size” and “the zip file actually contains what you think it contains” are two different claims, and I’d rather find out the hard way in a sandbox than the harder way in front of a client.

The lesson here isn’t subtle: whatever environment you’re building this kind of thing inside, don’t assume it’s a permanent home. Treat every meaningful piece of work as something that needs a real, verified copy living somewhere else, before you need it, not after.

The question that seemed simple: “can the whole team actually use this?”

Once the pipeline worked, the obvious next question arrived: this is genuinely useful — how does everyone else on the team get to use it, from inside the same chat interface, without each person needing their own separate copy of six skill folders sitting in their own individual environment?

My first answer was wrong, and I want to walk through exactly how, because the correction is more instructive than the original idea.

There’s a real, well-documented way to package multiple skills into a single, versioned, installable unit — a manifest file, a folder structure, a marketplace you can point at and install from with a single command. I researched it properly, checked the actual technical requirements against the real skill files, confirmed nothing would break in the process, and wrote out a complete, step-by-step plan for building it.

It was a good plan for the wrong tool. That entire packaging mechanism belongs to a developer-facing, command-line version of this technology — built for someone working from a terminal on their own machine, not for a team collaborating inside a shared chat interface. The two are genuinely separate systems: skills built for one don’t automatically show up in the other, and nothing about installing a package on a command line puts anything into a chat window at all. I’d built a complete, technically correct answer to a question nobody had actually asked.

There’s a real difference underneath that mistake worth pulling apart, because it’s not just “two systems with different plumbing” — it’s two different ways of actually building the thing in the first place, and they suit different people doing different jobs.

A skill built through a command-line tool is written the way software is normally written: someone opens a file, writes instructions, saves, tests, commits. It rewards someone comfortable in that environment, and it’s genuinely well-suited to a developer maintaining a tool for other developers.

Everything in this piece happened the other way. Every one of these six skills was written, argued with, broken, and rewritten entirely in natural language, inside the same chat window where the actual work was happening — often in the middle of a real task, the moment a real mistake surfaced. There was no separate “build” step and “use” step. The fixing happened in the same breath as the failing. For the actual audience this was built for — analysts, consultants, and reviewers who think in RFPs and staffing models, not in pull requests — that’s not a lesser way of building something. It’s the only way that audience would ever have built it at all. The command-line version demands you already be a developer before you can start. The chat-native version only demands that you can describe, clearly, what went wrong and what should happen instead — which is a much larger group of genuinely capable people.

That’s the real argument for why this way of building suits enterprise chat users better, not just differently: it puts the ability to fix the system in the hands of the people who actually notice when it’s wrong.

The real answer, once I went looking properly, was already sitting inside the chat platform itself: on team and organization plans, a skill you’ve built can be shared directly — with specific colleagues, with a defined group, or with the entire organization — and it shows up in each recipient’s own skills list, right inside the same chat interface everyone already uses, no terminal, no installation step, no separate packaging format required. Upload once. Share it. Everyone toggles it on. Update it later, and everyone using it gets the update automatically, without doing anything themselves.

That’s the version worth knowing about if you’re trying to bring something like this to an actual team of people who live in a chat window all day, rather than a command line. It’s less impressive-sounding than “install our custom plugin marketplace.” It’s also the one that actually reaches the people you built this for.

What this actually proves

I don’t think the takeaway here is that AI is about to replace anyone doing this kind of work. What I watched happen, across dozens of real conversations, was narrower and — to me — more interesting: six connected pieces of plain-English instruction, built and refined entirely through natural conversation by someone who never wrote a line of application code, correctly handled a genuinely complex, high-stakes, real piece of work. Hundreds of real applications, classified correctly on evidence rather than assumption. Thousands of real support tickets, read and understood well enough to catch two of its own file-reading mistakes before they became wrong numbers in a real deliverable. A staffing estimate, a commercial structure, and a leadership brief, assembled from real data, with every gap named honestly instead of quietly filled in with a plausible-sounding guess.

It’s also, genuinely, still young. The coordination between skills is held together by prose being read correctly, not a guaranteed contract. Getting smarter costs real context weight. The environment it runs in isn’t guaranteed to remember what you built inside it, unless you go out of your way to make sure it does. None of that is a reason to dismiss it. It’s the actual, honest shape of what building with this looks like right now — worth knowing precisely, rather than either oversold or waved away.

I’d rather tell you both halves of that than just the part that makes a better headline.

medium.titulo: Reporting Shouldn’t Be the Model’s Job
medium.resumo: We gave Claude Code sessions an org chart. Then one live run falsified four assumptions our test suite had already blessed.
medium.conteudo_html:
We gave Claude Code sessions an org chart. Then one live run falsified four assumptions our test suite had already blessed.

If you run more than one Claude Code session at a time, you have almost certainly tried the obvious thing: tell one of them to go manage the others.

It works for about five minutes.

We tried it repeatedly, across different projects, and it failed the same way every time. Eventually we stopped treating it as a prompting problem and started treating it as an architecture problem. This is what we found, what we built, and — more usefully — the six harness behaviours no unit test could have caught, four of which surfaced only when a real session ran.

Three failures, not one

The obvious symptom is that subordinates don’t report. You tell a session “let me know when you’re done,” and it doesn’t. But that is only the first of three failures, and it is the least interesting one.

Subordinates don’t report. The instruction lives in the model’s context. Context gets compacted, exhausted, or simply outcompeted by the task itself. By the time the work is finished, the instruction to report has been squeezed out by four hundred lines of test output. This is not a discipline problem. It is a memory-hierarchy problem, and no amount of better phrasing fixes it.

Supervisors can’t observe. This one is easy to miss. A Claude Code session only executes while a user turn is running. Between turns it is inert — it isn’t polling, isn’t waiting, isn’t thinking. So even a subordinate that does report has nobody awake to receive the report. The message lands in a session that will not read it until you, the human, type something.

Nothing notices failure. Two sessions edit the same file and silently clobber each other. A session runs out of context mid-task and dies. Another gets stuck in a loop. From the outside, all three look identical to a session that is simply taking a while.

The third failure is the one that actually costs you time, and it is the one every “just tell it to report back” approach ignores entirely.

The reframe

Here is the shift that made the rest tractable:

Reporting must not be something the model does. It must be something that happens to the model.

If the report depends on the model choosing to file it, the report is only as reliable as the model’s remaining context. Move it out of the model’s control and it becomes as reliable as the process lifecycle.

Claude Code gives you exactly the hook for this. A Stop hook fires when a session finishes a turn — executed by the harness, not by the model. Whether the model remembered, ran out of context, or died halfway, the hook runs.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "node",
            "args": ["${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stop-report.mjs"],
            "timeout": 15
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

That is the entire load-bearing idea. Everything else we built is scaffolding around it.

What we built

NestManager runs Claude Code sessions as an organisation: an Executive that talks to you, Managers that own workstreams, Staff that do the work. Roles are positional rather than fixed — a Staff member that hires its own team becomes a Manager for that subtree.

                          you
                           ▲
            results ───────┼─────── objective
                           ▼
                 ┌───────────────────┐
                 │     Executive     │
                 └─────────┬─────────┘
             ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
             ▼                           ▼
       ┌───────────┐               ┌───────────┐
       │  Manager  │               │  Manager  │
       └─────┬─────┘               └─────┬─────┘
        ┌────┴────┐                 ┌────┴────┐
        ▼         ▼                 ▼         ▼
     ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐           ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐
     │Staff│   │Staff│           │Staff│   │Staff│
     └──┬──┘   └──┬──┘           └──┬──┘   └──┬──┘
        └─ peers ─┘                 └─ peers ─┘

Every member reports to exactly one supervisor, and escalation travels one hop at a time. Peers settle overlapping work between themselves, and only involve a Manager when they can’t.

Three pieces are worth explaining, because each one encodes a decision that could have gone differently.

State is an append-only event log. Up to a dozen OS processes write to the same directory at once. Rather than locking, every state change is a single appended line, which is atomic at the OS level. The org chart is not stored — it is a projection folded from the log on read. A session that is force-killed cannot corrupt anything; worst case it leaves a stale working record, which is exactly what stall detection exists to catch.

Supervisors chase. Every supervisor classifies its direct reports on every turn, and escalates through a fixed ladder: nudge, read the transcript, reassign. The middle step matters more than it looks. A long test run and an infinite loop are indistinguishable from the outside; you have to read the actual output to tell them apart, and that judgement belongs to a model, not to a timeout.

Budgets are chained and denominated in dollars. This one drew an objection from a colleague — for a subscription user, dollars are abstract, and tokens are the unit you actually feel. We still chose dollars, for two reasons. --max-budget-usd is the only cap the harness will actually enforce; a token ceiling is a number in a JSON file that nothing is obliged to respect. And tokens are not comparable across model tiers: the same million tokens differ in cost by roughly an order of magnitude between the cheapest and most capable model. A token budget therefore cannot bound a hierarchy whose entire purpose is mixing tiers — a manager could stay comfortably inside it while multiplying the bill tenfold. Tokens are recorded as a gauge; dollars are the constraint.

The state a clock cannot see

Stall detection sounds like a timeout problem. It mostly is. But the most urgent state in the whole system is invisible to every silence-based check:

A member that reports blocked has just spoken.

Its last-heard-from timestamp is zero seconds ago. Every idle-time check rates it perfectly healthy. Meanwhile it has stopped working entirely and is waiting for a decision only its supervisor can make — and nothing will ever flag it, because it did the polite thing and told you it was stuck.

We found this in our own smoke test, before any of the harder bugs. A subordinate reported blocked: beyond_capability and the supervisor's status view cheerfully listed it as OK. The fix is trivial once you see it; seeing it is the part that took a live run.

Then we ran it for real

Here is where the article earns its keep.

At this point we had 74 unit tests, all green. CI passed on Linux and Windows, across two Node versions. The design held together on paper and in the test suite. We were confident.

Then we launched one real background session with a trivial task — create a file containing the word “hello” — and watched it fail four times in a row, for four unrelated reasons. None of them were coding errors. Every one was the harness behaving differently from how we had assumed, and every one failed silently.

1. --session-id is ignored for background sessions

We had designed identity around a simple idea: the parent assigns the child’s session ID upfront, so the org chart is written before the child exists and there is never a window where a subordinate is running but unregistered. Deterministic, clean.

claude --bg --session-id <uuid> does not use that UUID. The background session generates its own.

The consequence was almost poetic. The Stop hook looked up the harness’s session ID, found no matching member in the org chart, and returned without filing anything. The one mechanism whose entire job was guaranteeing a report was the thing that quietly did nothing.

The fix: pass the parent’s assigned ID through an environment variable and treat that as authoritative, falling back to the harness ID only when it is absent.

2. A background session has nobody to answer a permission prompt

Our subordinate followed its brief perfectly. It read its assignment, understood the protocol, and ran its first command — nest inbox — exactly as instructed.

Then it stopped, forever, on a permission prompt. --permission-mode acceptEdits covers file edits but not shell commands, and there is no human attached to a background session to click "Yes."

From the supervisor’s side this is indistinguishable from a stalled member. The subordinate is in fact doing everything right, waiting for an approval that cannot arrive.

The fix: pre-authorise the CLI at spawn time with --allowedTools. Note that you need both shell tools listed — which one a model reaches for is platform-dependent, PowerShell on Windows and Bash elsewhere.

3. --allowedTools is variadic and will eat your prompt

Having added the permission rules, we spawned again. The session started and immediately reported: idle — send a prompt to start.

--allowedTools <tools...> is variadic. It keeps consuming arguments past a boolean flag. So this:

claude --allowedTools "Bash(node:*)" --bg "<the actual prompt>"

swallows the prompt into the tools list and launches a session with no instructions at all, waiting patiently for input that will never come.

It stops cleanly at an option that takes a value of its own, so this works:

claude --allowedTools "Bash(node:*)" --model haiku --bg "<the actual prompt>"

We now emit the rules first, immediately before --session-id, so correctness doesn't depend on argument order elsewhere in the command.

4. Background sessions want a worktree before editing

Fourth attempt. The session announced: “I need to enter a worktree for this background session before making edits.” It tried to create one, failed because our scratch repository had no commits (Failed to resolve base branch "HEAD"), then tried to git commit — which needed an approval nobody could give.

Partly our test environment’s fault. But the underlying fact is real and worth knowing: background sessions lean toward worktree isolation for writes. Isolation is closer to a default than an option.

And two we found by probing rather than crashing

--append-system-prompt-file exists but is undocumented. It doesn't appear in claude --help, but probing it returns option '--append-system-prompt-file <file>' argument missing rather than an unknown-option error. This matters more than it sounds: a role brief is about thirty lines containing quotes and newlines, and passing that inline breaks three separate ways on Windows — cmd.exe cannot carry newlines in an argument, quote escaping differs across shells, and command lines cap at roughly 8191 characters. Writing the brief to a file and passing a path sidesteps all three.

--plugin-dir does not reach spawned sessions. Running a plugin from a clone applies to that session only. Sessions it spawns start with no hooks and no role skills — they ignore a protocol they were never handed. An installed plugin has no such problem, which is why installing properly is the recommended path and why the config carries an explicit forwarding option for the clone case.

The green suite wasn’t enough either

One more, because it cuts against the easy conclusion that “you just need live tests.”

Our CI caught a bug that our local runs never did. Events in the log were ordered by millisecond timestamp, with ties broken by a random event ID. On a fast machine a burst of events routinely lands in a single millisecond — so nudge, nudge, report could fold as report, nudge, nudge, leaving a member that had just reported still counted as un-nudged. The projection was non-deterministic, and it read differently on every load.

Locally, on Windows, 74 tests passed. On Linux, CI went red twice.

The fix was not finer-grained timestamps. Appends are atomic, so the physical line order in the file is the write order across every process. Tie-break on line index and the ordering becomes both deterministic and causally correct.

What we’d take from this

The lesson isn’t “AI-assisted development is unreliable.” The code was the cheap part and it was mostly right.

The lesson is about where confidence comes from. A green test suite tells you the system behaves as you modelled it. It says nothing about whether your model of the platform is correct — and every one of the failures above lived in that gap. Unit tests couldn’t have caught them, because the tests encoded the same wrong assumptions as the implementation.

What worked was making falsification cheap and then doing it repeatedly. Four live runs, each taking a few minutes and costing almost nothing on the smallest model, found four architectural defects that 74 tests had blessed.

If you are building on top of an agent platform, budget for that loop explicitly. The interesting bugs are not in your code. They are in the seam between your code and a harness whose behaviour you inferred rather than verified.

We wrote up all eight harness behaviours in docs/harness-notes.md, separately from the design spec, because they are facts about Claude Code rather than decisions about our project. If you are building anything on Claude Code, that file is probably more useful to you than the project itself.

NestManager is MIT licensed and on GitHub: github.com/tecnonest/NestManager

It is early — version 0.1.0, and we mean the 0.x. Issues and contributions welcome, particularly from anyone who has hit these walls from a different direction.

medium.titulo: How I Built and Shipped a Real App as a Solo Developer
medium.resumo: Vue 3, Supabase, and an AI planner that kept "forgetting" to call its own tools — lessons from shipping MiniMeals solo.
medium.conteudo_html:
How I Built MiniMeals: From Idea to Deployment

The problem that started it all

Every parent of a young child knows the feeling: it’s Sunday evening, and the week’s meal plan still doesn’t exist. Add allergies and dietary restrictions to the mix, and try putting together a shopping list without forgetting anything. And if a doctor or dietitian is monitoring the child, you also need some way to share what they’re actually eating.

That’s how MiniMeals came to be — a mobile-first app for planning a child’s meals, with a separate mode for doctors.

If you want to see the result, MiniMeals is live at https://minimeals.me — free to try, no credit card required.

The stack — and why

I deliberately picked a “boring,” proven stack instead of chasing hype:

  • Vue 3 + TypeScript + Vite for the core app — fast, type-safe, and the Composition API maps cleanly onto store logic
  • Pinia for state — one store per domain entity (recipe.store.ts, weekPlan.store.ts, friends.store.ts, etc.)
  • Supabase as the backend — Postgres + Auth + Storage + Edge Functions, no need to run my own server
  • TailwindCSS v4 with a single @theme for design tokens shared between the app and the landing page
  • Astro for the marketing landing page (minimeals.me) — static build, zero unnecessary JS
  • Fly.io for hosting the landing page (nginx in a Docker container)

The guiding principle: don’t add a framework or service until there’s a real need. The landing page still has no backend of its own — the contact form writes directly into a Supabase table using the public anon key, protected by RLS policies (INSERT only).

Architecture: family, child, doctor

The core data model isn’t “user” — it’s “child.” A single account can manage multiple child profiles, each with its own allergies and dietary restrictions. The weekly plan, shopping list, and allergy checks are all scoped to a specific child, not to the parent.

The doctor role is handled separately. A doctor doesn’t get automatic access to anything — the family has to explicitly invite a specific doctor, and only then can that doctor see the weekly plan and the child’s “tasted” foods, enforced through an is_doctor_of() RLS function rather than frontend checks.
If you want to see the result, MiniMeals is live at https://minimeals.me — free to try, no credit card required.

The AI assistant: the hardest part

The “ask AI to generate a week of meals” feature looks simple from the outside, but underneath it’s an Edge Function running Claude through a tool-calling loop (set_meal_slot, create_recipe, search_ingredients).

The trickiest bug I ran into: the model would sometimes announce an intention in plain text (“Now I’ll create the recipe…”) without ever actually calling the tool — and the turn would silently end with nothing done. The fix wasn’t trivial: the loop now tracks expectedTargets (the exact list of slots that still need to be filled) and nudges the model to continue — but only until that list is satisfied, otherwise the AI would wander off and start planning extra days nobody asked for.

Small bugs that ate hours of debugging

Two stories for the “non-obvious bugs” collection:

  1. Ad blockers were killing a component just because of its name. The BetaBanner.vue component broke the app for a chunk of users — ad blockers were filtering anything with "Banner" in the filename or network requests. Fix: rename it to BetaNotice.vue.
  2. The Edge Functions CLI deploy returned a 403 for no obvious reason — even with owner-level project access and a fresh token. The working fallback: copy the file manually via the Supabase Dashboard → Edge Functions → Code, and always paste it straight from disk (Get-Content -Raw | Set-Clipboard), because retyping it manually from a chat transcript silently corrupts identifiers.

Deployment

The landing page lives on Fly.io — a static Astro build served by nginx in a Docker container on port 8080, with www and the legacy fly.dev domain redirecting to the custom minimeals.me domain. The main app and Supabase functions follow a separate release cycle, with npx vue-tsc --noEmit required to pass clean before any phase is marked done.

What I took away from this project

  • RLS isn’t “extra security” — it’s the foundation of the architecture. Trusting frontend checks is trusting the attacker.
  • AI features fail differently than regular code — they “half-work,” and those half-failures are the hardest to catch with tests.
  • The dumbest bugs (ad blockers vs. the word “Banner”) are often the most expensive to debug.

MiniMeals is still under active development, and I’ll keep sharing real technical details from the journey.
If you want to see the result, MiniMeals is live at https://minimeals.me — free to try, no credit card required.

medium.conteudo_html:
One codebase, two very different experiences, and a quarter to move both onto Vue 3 — while shipping a revamp on top of it. Here is the plan we made, the proof of concept that de-risked it, and the numbers that came out the other side.

At Freshworks Marketplace, we have leveraged a single codebase to power two distinct experiences: a unified in-product gallery and a public website. Despite their differing natures, we have designed them in a manner that ensures a consistent UI across both experiences.

Our gallery experience is developed as a single-page application using Vue.js powered with Vue CLI, Vue Router, Vuex, and deployed to AWS S3. On the other hand, our website is a server-side rendered application powered by Nuxt.js and deployed to S3.

You can read the full story behind our decision to use a single codebase here.

While we have enjoyed the benefits of using a monorepo to help with this unique problem, it has also presented its own set of tradeoffs. One such challenge we encountered was migrating our entire codebase to the latest versions of the components in our tech stack. To make things more interesting, around the same time we recognized the need to improve the user experience through a major revamp. Our latest revamp features prominent filters, upgraded search capabilities, eye-catching colors, better use of available real estate, and a streamlined user interface that’s intuitive and easy to use. With these enhancements, our platform now provides an even more user-friendly experience than ever before. This post summarizes our learnings and the approaches that worked for us during this journey.

Getting started

On February 7, 2022, Vue 3 was announced as the new major version for Vue.js. Having heavily invested in Vue.js since 2018, we were eager to learn about the new upgrades and advancements from this community-led project.

Prior to this launch, back in February 2021, the first stable release of Vite JS caused a stir on Twitter. On one of the regular knowledge-sharing sessions we hold internally, we covered Vite and studied its potential very closely. This session prompted a proposal from one of our engineering managers to explore its use for our platform.

Since then, we have actively sought opportunities to integrate Vite into our workflow. It was a pleasant surprise to discover that Vite has been adopted as the official build toolchain for Vue 3. Meanwhile, we noticed that other important tools like Pinia for state management and Vitest for testing paired up with Vue 3 after gaining popularity as the defaults in many developer toolchains. This momentum presents a promising opportunity for us to become early adopters of Vue 3 and grow together with the community.

We wasted no time and began our experimentation immediately.

What made this upgrade critical to us?

Vue 3 is faster, smaller, more maintainable and it’s easier to target native.
— Evan You

As stated earlier, Vue 3 was set to become the new default version, and it is expected that support for Vue 2 will end by December 31, 2023. Vue 3 introduces several unforeseen modifications to its fundamental principles and APIs, diverging from previous updates. This necessitates progress in all other areas of the framework, which would soon push our current toolset into maintenance mode. This, in turn, could result in a growing number of security issues that are challenging to handle. Additionally, the latest upgrade pledges significant performance enhancements and a complete shift in API methodology, further emphasizing its significance.

Additionally, Vue 3 offers the following advantages that we particularly cared about:

  • Smaller Vue core: Size improvement reached by the combination of greater code modularity, a smaller core runtime, and a tree-shaking-friendly compiler. Thus the new core would be reduced from about 20KB to 10KB gzipped.
  • Better rendering performance: The Vue 3 renderer improves the performance of the rendering process by using optimizations such as the hoisting and inlining of static parts and implementing Vue 3’s reactivity with ES6 proxies.
  • Blazing fast, Vite-powered build toolchain.
  • More ergonomic Composition API syntax via script setup.
  • Improved TypeScript IDE support for Single File Components (SFCs) via Volar.
  • Command-line type checking for SFCs via vue-tsc.
  • Simpler state management via Pinia.
  • New dev tools extension with simultaneous Vue 2 / Vue 3 support and a plugin system that allows community libraries to hook into the dev tools panels.

You can read more about what’s new in Vue 3 here.

All the above factors provided enough persuasion to take on the challenge of being an early adopter for Vue 3. As an early adopter, with few proven examples to benchmark against, we also recognized the responsibility with which we must undertake this exercise.

It is important to keep in mind that there are likely to be some compatibility issues with existing code and third-party libraries during any major upgrade. It is therefore essential to conduct thorough research and take gradual steps. Also, staying current with the latest framework updates and changes is vital, as they are subject to frequent modifications from early feedback.

Planning the migration

By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail.

Before embarking on this large-scale migration, it was important to have a plan. We needed to get down to the level of tasks and their estimated timelines because we had planned marketing activity around the revamped design. The plan is particularly crucial in our case, as our repository is a monorepo that supports two distinct user experiences and therefore requires due consideration of how different components interplay across the stack.

We eventually came up with the following list of high-level items as part of the migration plan:

  • Upgrading from Vue version 2 to Vue version 3 (first for the in-product experience).
  • Upgrading from Nuxt version 2 to Nuxt version 3 (for the website).
  • Upgrading the build tooling from Vue CLI to Vite.
  • Migrating from the Options API to the Vue Composition API.
  • Switching from Vuex to Pinia for state management.
  • Eliminating the use of Element UI in several places on the UI in favor of Freshworks’ own design library Crayons.

As many of the above-listed items are relatively new to the community, the learning curve will undoubtedly be steep. Therefore, meticulous planning and prior experimentation were deemed to be necessary.

Consequently, we opted to begin with a comprehensive analysis of the migration and its impact on the existing codebase. Through this process, we were able to provide an approximate estimation of the required efforts and timelines.

Analysis

Although we have compiled a list of the action items, it is crucial to examine and comprehend the following points:

  • How would each item benefit us?
  • Why is it necessary to take each of these items into account, and are there any items that we can do without?
  • The level of effort required for each item, and whether we can accommodate it in terms of timelines.

In order to address these questions, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of each topic and documented our findings in a clear and concise manner on our internal wiki. This served as a learning center for future developers who would work on this upgraded codebase and facilitated a comprehensive peer review.

We also created a comprehensive checklist, which included a table estimating each task, and shared it with the team for initial feedback. This exercise allowed us to visualize the resources required and potential challenges and opportunities at the outset. As a result of this exercise, we made some helpful discoveries.

  • We identified noncritical UI updates that could wait for subsequent releases, allowing us to better allocate our time.
  • We compiled a list of backend requirements in advance, providing clarity on each item and enabling our backend team to work on the list in parallel.
  • This also provided an opportunity for our team to suggest some long-standing tech debt items that could potentially be paired if deemed relevant and beneficial.

The experimentation

A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
— Chinese proverb

Now that we had completed the analysis phase, the next step was to experiment with the code. Our Marketplace boasts over a thousand apps built by developers from around the globe. Before we rocked this boat, we decided to conduct a proof of concept (POC) prior to committing to a switch.

As part of the POC, we evaluated the following factors:

  • The overall development experience with the new APIs.
  • The ease of transition between the Options and Composition APIs.
  • Any blockers related to the current bundling mechanism, SSR, etc.
  • Would TypeScript be beneficial at this scale?
  • Potential pitfalls in migrating from Vue CLI to Vite.
  • How Crayons fits in with SSR, and any potential blockers.
  • How the new state-management library works with our current data model.

While we were experimenting with the changes, the state of Nuxt was not entirely stable. Nuxt 3 was in the Release Candidate stage, and as a result, we found ourselves in a position to decide whether to adopt Nuxt 3 immediately or wait for the stable release.

The problem with not updating the Nuxt version is that we would lose the flexibility of having components in common between our in-app and website experiences. The monorepo architecture is intended to reuse components as much as possible, but if our website continues to use Nuxt 2, it will not be able to understand the Vue 3 APIs that are part of our reusable components.

We had two options:

  1. Experiment with the Nuxt Release Candidate and proceed with the migration.
  2. Create a duplicate of common components that will remain in Vue 2 to be consumed by the website service.

The second option is clearly not scalable in the long term and will result in unnecessary rework in the future.

We engaged three committed engineers who would travel with us through this release journey. One of these engineers, who had previously presented a Vite experiment in our internal knowledge-sharing session, would be responsible for conducting the POC, which would be supported and reviewed by two of our leads. The POC was carried out in stages.

Phase 1: We experimented with Vue 3 APIs, focusing solely on the in-product experience. We migrated only the homepage as a standalone app to better evaluate the DX and identify any potential issues.

Phase 2: This involved experimenting with Nuxt 3 RC to determine its suitability. Since the framework was not yet fully stable, conducting an in-depth experiment was crucial.

We created a separate clone for this POC in a private repository, and our lead and architects thoroughly examined the code. We also included it as a demo item in our weekly sprint demo and collected feedback from the entire team.

Outcomes of the POC

Phase 1:

  • APIs and store: Our homepage successfully utilized multiple API calls and a significant portion of our data store, covering almost all new APIs including Composition API, Pinia store, async API calls, etc. No blockers or disparities were encountered with existing features.
  • Third-party dependencies: Certain unnecessary third-party dependencies were identified and removed, reducing our node-modules burden. Essential dependencies such as Fuse.js and Vue I18n were fitting in as expected. Deprecated dependencies such as Node Sass were also identified and replaced with alternatives such as Dart Sass.

Phase 2:

  • Nuxt 3: The experiment of using Nuxt 3 RC with Vue 3 APIs under the hood was relatively simple and encountered no major issues.
  • Fetch API: We identified an opportunity to replace Axios with simple HTTP fetch APIs as our calls mainly involve reading data from simple static JSON files.
  • Third-party dependencies: We evaluated critical third-party dependencies being used in the Nuxt project, and most of those turned out to be working as expected.
  • Nuxt Bridge: Nuxt Bridge (a forward-compatibility layer that allows you to experience many of the new Nuxt 3 features by simply installing and enabling a Nuxt module) was also evaluated but found to be unsuitable for our purpose, as it caused issues in the build process.

Stages of migration

Although we were now quite confident about the migration thanks to the learnings from the POC, it was crucial to plan the stages in which the migration would occur. As a team, we try to avoid big-bang changes and deployments unless there is no alternative available.

The idea was to gradually ship the migration in stages to ensure a smooth transition without any breakage in production. The stages we came up with are represented in the picture below.

Phase 1: The first stage involves migrating the code to Vue 3 without affecting the UI. This can be done separately from the UI revamp, which takes longer and requires a separate release.

Phase 2: After implementing the Vue 3 code, we had the option of gradually upgrading the UI, but we ultimately decided to release the updated in-product experience all at once. We made this decision based on the quick completion of the earlier phase, which allowed us to save bandwidth and avoid inconveniencing users with inconsistent UI differences.

Phases 3 and 4: The website experience remains unchanged until this phase, where the migration from Nuxt 2 to Nuxt 3 is carried out, similar to the in-product migration in Phase 1.

Phases 3 and 4 were eventually done in parallel, building on the knowledge gained in the earlier stages to fast-track progress. The refreshed website experience can be viewed at freshworks.com/apps.

Tech debts

In addition to the aforementioned steps, we recognized the potential for improvement in other areas such as productivity, performance, and build times.

Build setup: To optimize our build pipeline and accommodate our growing scale, we transitioned from a multi-branch to a single-branch repo structure, adopting the proven trunk-based development methodology for monorepos. Our repo now consists of a single master branch, with tags created for each environment. This allows us to leverage trunk-based development and deploy changes incrementally across different environments.

IDE setup: We upgraded our IDE setup to align with the new set of tools introduced. Previously, we relied on vetur in conjunction with VSCode. The recommended IDE setup now is VSCode with the Volar extension. This extension supports syntax highlighting, TypeScript, and IntelliSense for template expressions and component props. Additionally, Volar’s VSCode extension provides out-of-the-box formatting for Vue Single File Components, which made it an ideal choice for our setup.

Security: Also as a result of this upgrade, the number of security vulnerabilities decreased significantly, with critical vulnerabilities virtually eliminated.

Metrics on DX improvements

From a developer productivity perspective, we noticed significant gains from this upgrade, which are shared below for reference.

Comparison: in-product

Version                       Dev server start    Build time
Old gallery (Vue 2, Vue CLI)  ~8609 ms            ~36.70 s
New gallery (Vue 3, Vite)     ~807 ms             ~9.5 s

Comparison: website

Version                 Dev server start          Build time
Old website (Nuxt 2)    ~40.41 s                  ~80 s
New website (Nuxt 3)    ~5010 ms (Vite + nuxi)    ~74.42 s

Vulnerability audit: in-product + website monorepo

Before upgrade    After upgrade
Packages audited       2445              1645
Total vulnerabilities  90                5
Severity: Low          2                 0
Severity: Moderate     11                4
Severity: High         67                0
Severity: Critical     10                1

Learnings and takeaways

Our team managed to accomplish all of these improvements within a quarter by planning and experimenting beforehand. Despite facing a steep learning curve, we succeeded in delivering by remaining focused on our goal, sticking to the plan, learning quickly together, and staying aligned as a team.

For anyone planning a similarly major codebase migration, we recommend considering the following major takeaways from our experience.

  • We suggest analyzing each task item to determine priorities and understand the return on investment.
  • We also recommend conducting the migration in stages to avoid disrupting the pipeline and user experience.
  • Experiment with proofs of concept in areas that are unclear to minimize surprises.
  • Document and audit each stage to make the learning process easier for others on the team.

Good luck with your major migration!

Quarta-feira | 16 de setembro de 2026

A Autoridade Brasileira de Controle de Dopagem (ABCD) atualizou sua lista de atletas com suspensão provisória. Na nova listagem, consta o nome de Bianca Araújo Câmara, que participou da Live! 42k de Brasília no dia 2 de agosto. O exame detectou a presença das substâncias proibidas nandrolona e testosterona. Com a suspensão provisória, a atleta está impedida de participar de qualquer competição ou mesmo de assistir a eventos esportivos até a decisão final sobre o caso.

Corrida oficial do Iron Maiden em São Paulo

No dia 10 de outubro, São Paulo receberá a “Run For Your Lives”, a corrida oficial da banda Iron Maiden. O evento, que faz parte das celebrações da turnê mundial, acontecerá no Vale do Anhangabaú e contará com percursos de 5 km de corrida, 2,5 km de caminhada e uma corrida kids. A prova terá um trajeto inédito pelo centro histórico da cidade, passando por pontos como o Theatro Municipal, a Galeria do Rock e o Viaduto Santa Ifigênia. Após a corrida, haverá um show com a banda The Beast Experience, considerada um dos melhores covers de Iron Maiden do mundo. As vagas são limitadas e o segundo lote já está aberto. Utilize o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 para ter 10% de desconto na inscrição.

Maratona do Paraná abre inscrições para 2027

As inscrições para a Maratona Internacional do Paraná 2027 abrem hoje, dia 16 de setembro, às 14h. A prova, que faz parte do Circuito Brasil Gigante, será realizada entre os dias 26 e 28 de março de 2027, durante o feriado de Páscoa, em Pontal do Paraná. O evento terá distâncias de 5, 10, 21 e 42 km, além de um desafio especial. A Maratona do Paraná é uma das oito provas que compõem o circuito, que premiará os atletas que completarem todas as etapas.

Atualização sobre atleta trans em corrida de Limeira

Tivemos uma atualização sobre o caso da atleta que subiu no pódio feminino dos 5 km na 21k de Limeira. Após a denúncia de que se tratava de uma atleta trans, apuramos que a corredora Vitória, anteriormente Vinícius, de fato competiu na categoria feminina. A nova Norma 7 da CBAt proíbe que atletas que passaram pela puberdade masculina compitam em categorias femininas. Mesmo pela regra antiga, a transição deveria ocorrer antes da puberdade, o que não é permitido legalmente no Brasil. O erro, portanto, foi do delegado técnico da Federação Paulista de Atletismo, que deveria ter desclassificado a atleta. A responsabilidade recai sobre a federação, que não aplicou o regulamento corretamente.

Encontro no ASICS Run Challenge no Recife

Neste domingo, dia 20 de setembro, acontece a etapa de Recife do ASICS Run Challenge. A prova terá distâncias de 4, 7 e 15 km, e as inscrições ainda estão abertas. Estarei por lá para cobrir o evento e rever minha família. Quem for participar, pode usar o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 para garantir 10% de desconto.

Revelada a medalha da Maratona de Chicago

Foi divulgada a medalha da Maratona de Chicago 2026, que acontece no dia 11 de outubro. A peça traz o tradicional skyline da cidade na parte da frente e, no verso, os nomes dos 29 bairros pelos quais a prova passa. A fita também foi personalizada com as cores e símbolos do evento.
